title: What is the default mapping type in Elasticsearch (`_doc`), and why were multiple types removed?
shortTitle: The default mapping type in Elasticsearch (`_doc`) and why multiple types were removed

s1_definition.profdef: In older Elasticsearch, an index could contain multiple mapping types, which were named sub-groupings of documents within one index, loosely analogous to tables inside a database. Starting in version six, Elasticsearch deprecated multiple types and restricted each index to a single type, and from version seven onward that single type is the fixed, implicit value `_doc`. Multiple types were removed because they were a leaky abstraction: all types in one index shared the same underlying Lucene index, so fields with the same name across different types had to share one definition, which caused mapping conflicts, sparse storage, and confusing behaviour. The single `_doc` type eliminates that whole class of problems, and type-related URL segments and parameters have been progressively removed from the API.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India once kept savings customers and loan customers in the same ledger book but labelled each row as either a "savings" row or a "loan" row. The trouble was that both kinds of rows had to use the exact same column definitions, so if savings used "balance" as money and loans used "balance" as remaining principal with a different format, they clashed, and most rows left most columns blank. The bank eventually said: one ledger book holds exactly one kind of record, and if you need two kinds, keep two books. The single book type is like `_doc` — every record in an index is just "a document," with no competing sub-labels.
s1_definition.oneliner: Multiple types pretended to be separate tables but secretly shared one storage, so Elasticsearch replaced them with a single implicit type, `_doc`, and the rule "one index, one kind of document."
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** In older Elasticsearch, an index could contain multiple mapping types, which were named sub-groupings of documents within one index, loosely analogous to tables inside a database. Starting in version six, Elasticsearch deprecated multiple types and restricted each index to a single type, and from version seven onward that single type is the fixed, implicit value `_doc`. Multiple types were removed because they were a leaky abstraction: all types in one index shared the same underlying Lucene index, so fields with the same name across different types had to share one definition, which caused mapping conflicts, sparse storage, and confusing behaviour. The single `_doc` type eliminates that whole class of problems, and type-related URL segments and parameters have been progressively removed from the API.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India once kept savings customers and loan customers in the same ledger book but labelled each row as either a "savings" row or a "loan" row. The trouble was that both kinds of rows had to use the exact same column definitions, so if savings used "balance" as money and loans used "balance" as remaining principal with a different format, they clashed, and most rows left most columns blank. The bank eventually said: one ledger book holds exactly one kind of record, and if you need two kinds, keep two books. The single book type is like `_doc` — every record in an index is just "a document," with no competing sub-labels.

**One line to remember:** Multiple types pretended to be separate tables but secretly shared one storage, so Elasticsearch replaced them with a single implicit type, `_doc`, and the rule "one index, one kind of document."

sections.s2_technical:
To understand the change you need to know what a mapping type originally was. In Elasticsearch versions before six, you created an index and could define several types within it, for example a "customer" type and a "transaction" type in the same index. Each type had its own mapping describing its fields. People reached for this because it looked like a relational database where one database holds many tables, so they assumed one index could hold many types the same way.

The problem is that this analogy was false under the hood. In a relational database, two tables are genuinely independent: a column named "value" in one table has no relationship to a column named "value" in another. In Elasticsearch, all types within a single index were stored in the same Apache Lucene index. Lucene has no concept of types at all; it only sees fields. So if the "customer" type and the "transaction" type both had a field called "value," they were in fact the same Lucene field and had to share a single definition. If one wanted "value" to be a number and the other wanted it to be text, that was an irreconcilable mapping conflict, and Elasticsearch would reject it.

This shared-field reality caused several concrete problems. There were mapping conflicts, as just described, whenever two types used the same field name with different intended types. There was sparse storage and poor compression, because documents of the customer type left all the transaction-only fields empty and vice versa, so the single underlying index was full of blanks, which hurt both storage efficiency and the quality of certain internal statistics. And there was conceptual confusion, because developers reasoned about types as if they were isolated tables when they were not, leading to surprising behaviour.

Elasticsearch therefore began removing multiple types. In version six, an index was limited to a single type. In version seven, specifying a type in most API calls was deprecated, and the type effectively became a fixed internal value, `_doc`. The name `_doc` was chosen partly because it reads naturally in the document APIs and partly as a neutral placeholder meaning "a document," with no suggestion that you should create meaningful type names. In version eight, type references were removed from the APIs more completely, so you simply address an index and its documents without ever naming a type.

The practical migration guidance that replaced multiple types is straightforward: if you previously used two types in one index to model two kinds of entities, you now use two separate indices, one per entity kind, because separate indices are genuinely independent and each has its own field definitions with no sharing. If instead you have documents that are variations of the same kind and only sometimes differ, you keep them in one index and add a plain field, often called something like "type" or "category," to distinguish them, filtering on that field at query time. The difference is that this is now an ordinary field under your control, not a special structural concept with hidden shared-storage consequences.

The senior-level nuance is that this change reflects a broader principle: an abstraction that does not match its implementation is worse than no abstraction. Mapping types promised relational-style isolation but delivered shared Lucene fields, and that mismatch produced bugs and confusion for years. Removing them simplified the mental model to "an index is a collection of similar documents," which aligns exactly with how Lucene actually works. When you work with any modern Elasticsearch client, you will see the document APIs use the `_doc` endpoint, and you should treat the type as a vestigial constant rather than something to design around.
sections.s3_banking:
At National Bank of India, an older system tried to store both customer profiles and transaction records in a single Elasticsearch index using two mapping types. After an upgrade, the team must redesign to the modern single-type model.

Problem 1 — The customer type had a field "amount" meaning the customer's credit limit as a plain number, while the transaction type had a field "amount" meaning the money moved, which the team wanted formatted differently. Because both lived in one index, they were the same Lucene field and conflicted. This is exactly the mapping-conflict problem that multiple types caused.

Problem 2 — Customer documents left every transaction-only field blank and transactions left every customer-only field blank, so the single index was mostly empty cells. This is exactly the sparse-storage problem that motivated removing types.

Problem 3 — The team needs the modern design. Two genuinely different entities should live in two separate indices, each with its own clean mapping and no field sharing. This is exactly the replacement pattern for multiple types.

To make this runnable without a real cluster, we will build a small program that contrasts the old and new models. It will contain a `MappingRegistry` that simulates how a single shared index forces one definition per field name and detects a conflict, and an `IndexCatalog` representing the modern approach where each index has its own independent mapping under the fixed `_doc` type. The demo first reproduces the old conflict, then shows the modern design with separate customer and transaction indices resolving it cleanly.
sections.s4a_structure:
Project structure:

```
mapping-types-demo/
├── pom.xml
├── src/
│   ├── main/
│   │   ├── java/com/bank/mapping/
│   │   │   ├── MappingDemo.java                   (main class)
│   │   │   ├── legacy/
│   │   │   │   └── SharedIndex.java                (old multi-type model)
│   │   │   └── modern/
│   │   │       ├── IndexDefinition.java            (single _doc type)
│   │   │       └── IndexCatalog.java               (independent indices)
│   │   └── resources/
│   │       └── application.yml
│   └── test/
│       └── java/com/bank/mapping/
│           └── modern/
│               └── IndexCatalogTest.java
```

Configuration file:

```yaml
# application.yml — modern design: one index per entity, type is always _doc
indices:
  - name: customers
    type: _doc
  - name: transactions
    type: _doc
```
sections.s4e_build:
How you build and run it:

```bash
# Build and run the model
mvn clean package -DskipTests
java -jar target/mapping-types-demo-1.0.0.jar

# Modern real Elasticsearch: one index per entity, _doc is implicit
curl -X PUT "localhost:9200/customers" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"mappings":{"properties":{"amount":{"type":"long"}}}}'
curl -X PUT "localhost:9200/transactions" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"mappings":{"properties":{"amount":{"type":"scaled_float","scaling_factor":100}}}}'
# Index a document — note the _doc in the URL, no custom type
curl -X POST "localhost:9200/transactions/_doc" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"amount":50000,"account":"SAV2001"}'
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: an attempt to define a field named "amount" as a number for a customer type and as text for a transaction type in one legacy shared index, followed by the modern design using two separate indices.

Step 1: The legacy SharedIndex is created. The customer type defines the field "amount" as a long, which represents a credit limit stored as a number. The shared field map now records that "amount" is a long.

Step 2: The transaction type tries to define the same field name "amount" as text, because that type wanted the money value formatted as a string. Because all types in a legacy index share one underlying Lucene field, the code finds that "amount" is already defined as a long and detects an irreconcilable conflict.

Step 3: The conflict throws an exception, and the demo logs the failure with its full message. This reproduces exactly the real-world mapping conflict that multiple types caused: two "types" could never truly have independent definitions for a same-named field.

Step 4: The modern design begins. The IndexCatalog creates a "customers" index. Its single implicit type is `_doc`, and it owns its own field space. The customer index defines "amount" as a long with no interference from anything else.

Step 5: The catalog creates a separate "transactions" index, also with the implicit `_doc` type and its own independent field space. This index defines "amount" as a scaled float suited to money. Because the two indices are genuinely separate, the two definitions of "amount" never touch each other.

Step 6: The catalog describes both indices, showing each with type `_doc` and its own clean "amount" definition. The conflict that was unavoidable in the old model simply cannot occur in the new one, because separation is real rather than pretended.

Final output:

```text
Oct 25, 2026 2:45:09 AM com.bank.mapping.MappingDemo main
INFO: === legacy multi-type index ===
INFO: type 'customer' defined field 'amount' as long
SEVERE: legacy design failed: mapping conflict: field 'amount' already defined as 'long' (by another type) but type 'transaction' wants 'text'
INFO: === modern single-type design ===
INFO: created index 'customers' with type _doc
INFO: created index 'transactions' with type _doc
INFO: index 'customers' (type=_doc) fields={amount=long}
INFO: index 'transactions' (type=_doc) fields={amount=scaled_float}
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  OLD (multiple types, one index)
    index "bank"
      ├─ type "customer"    → field amount : long   ┐
      └─ type "transaction" → field amount : text    │  SAME Lucene field
                                                      ▼
                                         CONFLICT (shared storage) ✗

  NEW (single implicit type _doc, one index per entity)
    index "customers"    (_doc) → amount : long          ✓ independent
    index "transactions" (_doc) → amount : scaled_float  ✓ independent
      │
      ▼ query addresses index + _doc, never a custom type
    POST /transactions/_doc  {"amount":50000,...}
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
In older Elasticsearch, an index could contain multiple mapping types, which were named sub-groupings of documents inside one index that people treated like tables inside a database. From version six onward Elasticsearch deprecated multiple types and limited each index to a single type, and from version seven that single type became a fixed implicit value, `_doc`. So in modern Elasticsearch you never create meaningful type names; every document in an index is simply a `_doc`, and the document APIs reflect that with endpoints like slash index slash underscore doc.

The reason multiple types were removed is that they were a leaky abstraction. The relational analogy that one index could hold many independent types the way a database holds many independent tables was false under the hood. All types within one index were stored in the same Apache Lucene index, and Lucene has no concept of types at all — it only sees fields. So if two types both had a field named "amount," they were physically the same Lucene field and had to share one definition. If one wanted it as a number and the other as text, that was an irreconcilable mapping conflict. On top of that, documents of one type left all the other type's fields blank, producing sparse, poorly compressed storage, and the mismatch between the mental model and the reality caused years of confusing bugs.

The modern replacement is simple and I apply it directly. If I previously used two types in one index to model two genuinely different entities, I now use two separate indices, one per entity, because separate indices really are independent and each owns its own field definitions with no sharing. If instead I have documents that are variations of the same kind, I keep them in one index and add an ordinary field, perhaps called "category," to distinguish them and filter on it at query time — but that is now a normal field under my control, not a special structural concept with hidden shared-storage consequences.

At National Bank of India, we hit exactly this when an older system had crammed customer profiles and transaction records into one index using two types, and a field named "amount" meant a credit limit for customers but a money value for transactions, which collided. The fix was to split them into a customers index and a transactions index, each with the implicit `_doc` type and its own clean mapping, so "amount" could be a plain long in one and a scaled float in the other with no conflict. The broader lesson I take from it is that an abstraction which does not match its implementation is worse than no abstraction, and removing mapping types gave Elasticsearch a mental model — an index is a collection of similar documents — that finally matches how Lucene actually works.
